title: Layered architecture
summary: Split a use case into presentation, application, domain and data layers so each can be read, tested and changed on its own.
signals: a single function or class that parses input, applies a business rule and issues SQL
a business-rule test that must build a request object and a database to run at all
SQL or table/column names sitting next to validation or business logic
a rule change and a column rename both forcing an edit to the same function

roles.handleCancelRequest: presentation: parses the request into a command, calls the application layer, shapes a response
roles.CancelOrder: application: service that loads the aggregate, calls domain behaviour, and saves it
roles.Order.cancel(): domain: state transition that enforces the invariant
roles.OrderRepository: port: persistence contract owned by the application layer (get / save)
roles.SqliteOrderRepository: data: adapter over a real store, implementing the application's port
roles.InMemoryOrderRepository: data: test/demo adapter honouring the same contract

stages.title: Coupled
stages.idea: One function parses the request, applies the cancellation rule and runs SQL. Testing the rule needs a request record and a database.

stages.title: Layered
stages.idea: Presentation parses a request into a command and shapes a response; application orchestrates; domain owns the rule; data implements the application's repository port. Each layer is tested at its own level, plus one integration test through all four.

checks: Why does the presentation layer depend on the application layer's abstraction instead of a concrete class, and what does that let the handler's test skip?
Who owns the repository port here — the application layer or the data layer — and why does that ownership matter?
What's the difference between an application service that only forwards to the domain (an anemic service layer) and one that holds real orchestration logic?
When is a single function like the before stage's the right amount of layering, and when does it stop paying for itself?
